body.hook: Many of the most exciting plays are created by groups, not single writers. In playbuilding, an ensemble starts with an idea, improvises scenes, then shapes the best moments into an original play.

study.title: Build a Play
study.question: How does a group turn an idea into a structured play?
study.passage:
Playbuilding process (written for this lesson):
1. Starting point (10 minutes): Each group picks a stimulus: a photo (an empty swing), an object (a lost key), a headline ("Student finds wallet with $1,000"), a theme (belonging) or a question ("What would you risk for a friend?").
2. Brainstorm (10 minutes): Web the stimulus: characters, places, problems, secrets.
3. Improvise (15 minutes): Quickly improvise three 1-minute scenes from the web. Keep what works.
4. Structure (15 minutes): Shape the best ideas into a 5-scene outline on a dramatic structure arc: Scene 1, exposition (who, where, normal life); Scene 2, inciting incident (the problem appears); Scene 3, rising action (it gets worse); Scene 4, climax (the turning point); Scene 5, resolution (what changes). Give each scene a title, characters and a one-sentence summary. Total play length: 5–7 minutes.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Write a five-scene outline on a structure arc
discussion: What idea did your stimulus spark?
Which improvisation was strongest and why?
What is your play's central conflict?
study.product: Submit a five-scene outline with a title, character list, central conflict and one-sentence summary per scene.

body.objective: Students will be able to direct peers in a scene.

successCriteria: I can give clear, respectful direction to actors
I can use questions to help actors find choices

body.hook: A director is the person who sees the whole picture. They don't act; they watch, ask questions and help actors make choices that serve the story. Today some of you step into the director's chair.

vocabulary.definition: The person who guides actors and shapes the overall production.

study.title: The Director's Chair
study.question: How do directors help actors bring a scene to life?
study.passage:
Directing guide (written for this lesson):
1. Vision: Before rehearsing, the director writes one sentence: "This scene should feel ___ because ___."
2. Actor-friendly direction: Give actions, not results. Instead of "Be sadder," say "Try avoiding her eyes until the last line" or "What does your character want from him right now?"
3. Ask questions: "What just happened before you came in?" "What would happen if you didn't sit down?"
4. Stage picture: Step back and look. Can the audience see every face? Is the important moment downstage and in focus?
5. Run, stop, fix: Run a short section, stop, give one note, run it again. Don't give ten notes at once.
Task: In your playbuilding group, each member directs one scene of the outline for 10 minutes while the others act. Rotate. Directors record notes they gave and what changed.

body.objective: Students will be able to rehearse and revise a group play.
body.iCan: I can rehearse and revise a group play.
successCriteria: I can rehearse a full group play
I can revise the play based on feedback
I can perform an original play with polish
body.hook: The first time a group runs its original play from start to finish, things usually fall apart: scenes run long, transitions are messy, the ending doesn't land. That's normal. Revision is where the play gets good.

vocabulary.definition: Changing a play to improve it.
How the play moves from one scene to the next.
The written text of the play, including dialogue and stage directions.
A final full rehearsal with all elements.
The group working together as one.

study.title: Revise and Perform
study.question: How does revision turn a rough play into a strong performance?
study.passage:
Process (written for this lesson):
1. Script it (one lesson): Write down the dialogue that worked in improvisation, plus key stage directions. Keep it short; use your scene outline.
2. First full run (10 minutes): Time it. Note the running time.
3. Feedback (10 minutes): Another group watches and answers: Was the conflict clear? Where did it drag? Was the climax powerful? Did the ending feel complete?
4. Revision (20 minutes): Make at least three revisions. Common fixes: cut repeated lines; sharpen the climax; speed up transitions (use a freeze, music or a narrator line); make the ending clearer (a final image or line).
5. Dress rehearsal and performance: Perform for the class or another grade.
6. Reflection: What did your group change, and why did it make the play better?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Write a script from your outline and improvisations
discussion: What was your first running time?
What three revisions did you make?
How did the final performance compare with the first run?
study.product: Perform your revised group play and write a reflection describing three revisions and how each improved the play.

examples.title: Dragging scene
examples.problem: Scene 3 runs 3 minutes but the play is meant to be 6. Fix?
examples.answer: Cut repeated lines and keep only what moves the story
examples.explore: How do you decide what to cut?

examples.title: Transitions
examples.problem: Long silent gaps between scenes. Fix?
examples.answer: Use a freeze, a narrator line or music while actors move

examples.title: Climax
examples.problem: Feedback says the climax wasn't clear. Fix?
examples.answer: Slow it down, move it downstage centre and add a pause

examples.title: Ending
examples.answer: Add a final image or line that shows what has changed
